extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying the principles, limits, and proper methods of induction as set out in a logic textbook chapter—what induction is, what makes it legitimate, and how it differs from related operations (mathematical demonstration, mere aggregation, tests of inconceivability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is 'the operation of discovering and proving general propositions' — the process by which we infer that what is true in particular cases will be true in all cases which resemble them in assignable respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes that inference proceeds from the known to the unknown; the same principles apply whether the conclusion is an individual fact or a general proposition. 'Whenever the evidence which we derive from observation of known cases justifies us in drawing an inference respecting even one unknown case, we should on the same evidence be justified in drawing a similar inference with respect to a whole class of cases.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of an Induction depends on conditions of the instances
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction is legitimate only when the observed instances (in number and nature) sufficiently justify extending the predicate to the whole class; legitimacy is determined by those conditions which render the inference from observed to unobserved cases warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sufficiency of evidence 'depends on the number and nature of the instances, and not their being the whole of those which happen to be known.' One need not have examined every known instance to make a legitimate generalization; rather one must have appropriate representative and explanatory instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between true induction and mere abridgment ('perfect' induction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A process that merely summarizes every known individual (so that the conclusion contains nothing beyond the premises) is not genuine induction; genuine induction must infer beyond the particular facts recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of pseudo-induction: stating 'All the planets shine by the sun’s light' from observation of each planet (a mere summing up). True generalization affirms more than the sum of the special propositions from which it is inferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction requires inference (not mere registration or demonstration)
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic quality of induction is inferential extension from particular observed facts to unobserved cases; operations involving no such inference (mere registration of facts or mathematical demonstrations) are not induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Processes that simply condense singular propositions into general language (or prove a theorem for a diagram and then generalize because the reasoning applies generally) are not inductive in the sense used here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of appropriate inductions is a separate skill in practical inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: In practical contexts (e.g., advocacy, judging), the chief difficulty is choosing which general propositions or maxims to apply, not the abstract legitimacy of induction itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Success depends on sagacity and knowledge to 'bring his case under those propositions or principles' and to select the generalizations best adapted to the object; invention (finding which induction to use) cannot be reduced to fixed rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer testing propositions by experience rather than inconceivability
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of inconceivability (that the negation is inconceivable) is not a conclusive proof of truth; propositions should be tested by experience when possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Spencer: 'why should the truth be tested by the inconceivability, when we can go further back for proof—namely, to the experience itself?' Examples: sunrise/sunset mistaken conception, gravitation without medium, antipodes—cases once judged inconceivable yet false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on using inconceivability as a test (Spencer's Universal Postulate)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inability to conceive the negation of a proposition only shows inseparability of predicate and subject in thought, not necessarily inseparability in fact; the test applies (if at all) only to simple cognitions assented to on immediate inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if 'the predicate invariably exists along with the subject' in our conceptive faculty, this does not prove the predicate co-exists in actual Nature. The test is legitimately applicable only to propositions 'assented to on simple inspection, without any intervening media of proof.' Complex propositions require mediating proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of inconceivability-test limited to simple propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A test that appeals to inconceivability can only legitimately be applied to simple propositions where subject and predicate are in direct relation; it fails for complex propositions that require mediate argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: arithmetic/geometrical truths (e.g., square of hypothenuse) are complex and require mediate steps; schoolboy mistakes show failure may arise from inattention, not a flaw in the test itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and nature of instances, not exhaustiveness, determine inductive power
rubrics_metrics.description: What makes observed instances sufficient evidence for a general law is their number and the nature (representativeness, relevant diversity) of the instances rather than having examined every individual instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the nervous system example: if observations of various species show a nervous system, the inference that 'all animals have a nervous system' may be legitimate even without checking every known species, provided the instances are suitably representative and explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing induction from mathematical reasoning/demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical proofs and reasoning that produce universal propositions often do so by demonstrative (a priori) methods, not by induction from observed instances; such proofs are not the kind of inductive inference under discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagram-based geometric proofs or parity-of-reasoning arguments prove the theorem by demonstration; where a mathematical generalization appears to be based on examples, it rests on 'a priori considerations' or demonstrative reasoning rather than empirical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms (e.g., Principle of Contradiction) as generalizations from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Logical axioms like the Principle of Contradiction and (to a qualified extent) the Principle of Excluded Middle are grounded in generalization from mental and sensory experience, not merely verbal identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Principle of Contradiction arises from observation that 'Belief and Disbelief are two different mental states, excluding one another' and from contrasts like light/darkness, motion/quiescence—thus axioms are 'generalizations from all these facts.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification of the Principle of Excluded Middle (meaningfulness requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Principle of Excluded Middle (that a proposition must be either true or false) holds only when the predicate can be intelligibly attributed to the subject; otherwise a third possibility—'Unmeaning'—arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Abracadabra is a second intention' is neither true nor false. Extending Excluded Middle to Noumena (things in themselves) without qualification is illegitimate because predicates may not be intelligible of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: The logic of science (induction) is universal in scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The principles and rules of induction that establish general propositions in science are the same principles and rules that govern inductive inference in everyday practical life; therefore a complete logic of the sciences is the universal logic of inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because every legitimate inference from experience that yields either a fact or a general truth uses the same inductive principles, an analysis of induction is 'virtually an analysis of all induction whatever.' Examples drawn from astronomy show identical structure between proving individual facts and general laws.
